title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a significant but frequently underrecognized disorder in pediatrics, particularly among children with neurodevelopmental delay. The American Thoracic Society and the American Academy of Pediatrics define pediatric OSA as a sleep-related breathing disorder marked by recurrent partial or complete upper airway obstruction leading to disrupted ventilation and fragmented sleep.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: The condition arises from anatomical, neuromuscular, and inflammatory factors. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy represents the predominant etiology in younger children, whereas obesity is the leading cause in older children and adolescents. Risk factors include craniofacial anomalies, allergic rhinitis, neuromuscular weakness, and exposure to secondhand smoke. Snoring, restless sleep, behavioral changes, and daytime somnolence are common manifestations.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis hinges on clinical suspicion and is confirmed by overnight polysomnography, which quantifies apnea–hypopnea events. First-line management includes adenotonsillectomy, while weight reduction and treatment of comorbidities are recommended adjuncts. Continuous positive airway pressure therapy may be required for residual disease. Untreated OSA predisposes to cardiovascular, neurocognitive, and growth complications. Prognosis is generally favorable with early recognition and appropriate intervention.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to strengthen learners' proficiency in evaluating and managing pediatric OSA. Participants will advance their mastery of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Improved skills will equip clinicians to collaborate with interprofessional teams providing care for affected children.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical and diagnostic findings indicative of pediatric obstructive sleep apnea, paying attention to etiologic and modifiable risk factors to guide management. Apply evidence-based, individualized strategies for managing pediatric obstructive sleep apnea and mitigating its potential complications. Improve parental and caregiver awareness of the causes, symptoms, and consequences of pediatric obstructive sleep apnea to promote early recognition, adherence to treatment, and healthier sleep practices. Collaborate with all members of the interprofessional team, including specialists such as otolaryngologists, pediatricians, and sleep physicians, to provide efficient, comprehensive, and coordinated care for children with obstructive sleep apnea. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Introduction
content: Sleep is an active physiologic and neurologic process essential for multiple restorative functions. Adequate quantity and quality of sleep exert a significant influence on memory consolidation, cognitive performance, learning capacity, somatic growth, and cardiovascular health in children. Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) encompasses a spectrum of disorders characterized by increased upper airway resistance and pharyngeal collapsibility, ranging from primary snoring to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which may occur across all age groups. [1]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Introduction
content: Pediatric OSA is a sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, resulting in intermittent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and sleep fragmentation. The condition adversely affects behavior, neurocognitive development, metabolism, and overall health in children. Early recognition, thorough evaluation, and appropriate management are critical to preventing long-term sequelae. [2] This activity discusses the etiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic approach, prognosis, and management of OSA in children. The discussion of adult OSA is presented separately. [3]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Etiology
content: Sleep apnea is classified into 2 primary categories based on etiology: central and obstructive. [4] Central sleep apnea results from pathology within the central nervous system, characterized by impaired neurologically mediated respiratory drive without associated respiratory effort. OSA, which accounts for approximately 95% of diagnosed sleep apnea cases, results from the complete or partial collapse of the upper airway during sleep, leading to arousals or oxygen desaturation of 3% or greater.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Etiology
content: Any factor that reduces airway diameter or structural integrity may contribute to OSA, including anatomic, physiologic, genetic, environmental, and neuromuscular influences. Intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms increase upper airway collapse risk. Intrinsic factors involve the critical closing pressure required to maintain airway patency, whereas extrinsic factors include fat deposition, tissue hypertrophy, and craniofacial abnormalities that alter normal anatomy. Additional risk factors associated with pediatric OSA include male sex, history of prematurity, daycare attendance, lower socioeconomic status, and African American race (see Images . Etiology of Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea; Anatomical Differences in Pediatric Airway Related to Sleep Apnea). [5] [6]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Epidemiology
content: The incidence of pediatric OSA peaks between ages 2 and 8 years, coinciding with increased tonsillar and adenoidal growth relative to upper airway dimensions in this developmental period. The prevalence of OSA in children is estimated at 2% to 5%, though higher rates are observed in certain clinical populations. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy characterizes the classical form, which predominates in children aged 3 to 5 years. Obesity-related OSA, resembling the adult phenotype, is more prevalent in adolescents. Morphologic, structural, and congenital variants occur in genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, achondroplasia, and Pierre Robin sequence. Neuromuscular and lysosomal storage disorders also confer increased susceptibility across pediatric age groups. [7]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Epidemiology
content: In a study by Lumeng et al, habitual snoring was reported in 1.5% to 6% of children, apneic events in 0.2% to 4%, parent-reported SDB in 4% to 11%, and clinically diagnosed OSA in 1% to 4%. SDB was found to be more common in boys, children with higher body weight, and African American populations. The study identified insufficient age-specific prevalence data and recommended further epidemiologic investigation to better define pediatric SDB patterns. [8]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Diagnosis of OSA is established by quantifying apneic and hypopneic events during sleep. Specific diagnostic criteria are discussed in the Evaluation section.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Four principal factors contribute to the development of OSA: obesity, lymphoid hyperplasia, craniofacial abnormalities, and neuromuscular dysfunction. Each of these mechanisms increases extrinsic or intrinsic forces that compromise upper airway patency.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Obesity results in peripharyngeal fat deposition, which elevates extrinsic pressure and promotes airway collapse during sleep. Lymphoid hyperplasia, particularly tonsillar and adenoidal enlargement, narrows the airway lumen. Muscle relaxation during sleep exacerbates obstruction.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Neuromuscular dysfunction contributes to OSA through impaired airway tone and control. This pathophysiologic mechanism is frequently observed in conditions such as Down syndrome, where hypotonia increases airway collapsibility.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Craniofacial abnormalities further predispose to OSA. Syndromes such as Crouzon, Pierre Robin, and Apert, as well as cleft lip and palate, alter airway geometry and reduce posterior oropharyngeal space. Features including micrognathia, macroglossia, and midface hypoplasia contribute to structural narrowing and elevate the risk of upper airway obstruction during sleep.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Katz et al (2007) reviewed the pathophysiology of pediatric OSA, emphasizing the influence of craniofacial and soft tissue structures on upper airway dimensions. Narrowing and retropositioning of the maxilla and mandible predispose individuals to airway obstruction. Neuromuscular activation, arousal threshold, and ventilatory control further determine upper airway stability, which depends on the tonic activity of pharyngeal dilator muscles during wakefulness. Activation of these muscles decreases markedly during sleep. In rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, diminished pharyngeal dilator activity results from central REM-related processes. During nonrapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, reduced ventilatory drive following ventilatory overshoot leads to transient decreases in airway muscle tone and consequent obstructive events. [9]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pathophysiology
content: Congenital syndromes associated with craniofacial abnormalities frequently contribute to pediatric OSA. Pierre Robin sequence, Crouzon syndrome, and Apert syndrome cause micrognathia and glossoptosis, resulting in airway narrowing. Macroglossia and neuromuscular dysfunction in Down syndrome similarly predispose to airway obstruction. Children with Prader-Willi syndrome exhibit hypotonia, increasing airway collapsibility, while Treacher Collins syndrome leads to obstruction through facial skeletal deformities. In mucopolysaccharidoses, glycosaminoglycan accumulation within soft tissues of the airway produces mechanical narrowing (see Image . Pathologic Breathing Cycle in Obstructive Sleep Apnea). [10]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: Evaluation of sleep quantity and quality is an essential component of pediatric assessment. Studies indicate considerable variation in sleep screening practices across healthcare settings. Although no universally adopted screening tool exists specifically for pediatric OSA, current guidelines recommend that clinicians assess sleep quantity, quality, and the presence of snoring at every well-child visit. When poor sleep quality is suspected, additional questions should address frequent awakenings, abnormal sleep positioning, and disrupted bed coverings, which may indicate excessive nighttime movements. Parental reports are particularly valuable, as caregivers may not volunteer concerns regarding sleep without specific prompting. [11]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: Craniofacial abnormalities, specific syndromes, and early-life events increase the risk of OSA. Repeated screening is advised for patients with neuromuscular disorders, Down syndrome, and craniofacial malformations. Children with a history of prematurity also demonstrate an elevated risk for OSA, even in the absence of other predisposing factors. Studies have shown that up to 9.4% of school-aged children born prematurely are later diagnosed with OSA. Since these patients may not display the classic features of pediatric OSA, a low threshold for referral for polysomnography (PSG) is warranted. [12]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: Children often exhibit clinical manifestations that differ from the classic adult presentation of OSA, with behavioral changes being the most prominent distinguishing feature. Parents frequently report snoring, mouth breathing, witnessed apneas, frequent nighttime awakenings, and secondary nocturnal enuresis. Disrupted sleep in pediatric patients can manifest as hyperactivity, irritability, or aggression, which often leads caregivers to seek medical evaluation.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: Various tools and questionnaires have been developed to assess symptoms of OSA in both adults and children. The adult STOP-BANG questionnaire has been modified for adolescents as the Teen STOP-BANG screening tool. In this version, the question regarding “age greater than 50 years” is replaced with one addressing academic difficulties, as learning problems are a recognized symptom of SDB in children. The questionnaire consists of 8 yes-or-no questions, with scoring interpreted as follows: 0 to 2: Low risk 3 to 4: Intermediate risk 5 to 8: High risk Table 1 outlines the adaptations incorporated in the Teen STOP-BANG questionnaire (see Table 1 . Comparison of the Adult and Teen STOP-BANG Questionnaires). [13]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale has been adapted for pediatric use as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale for Children and Adolescents (ESS-CHAD). Janssen et al demonstrated in 2017 that the ESS-CHAD is a reliable and internally valid instrument for assessing daytime sleepiness in adolescents aged 12 to 18 years. Further studies were recommended to establish the tool's internal validity in children younger than 12 years, as well as to confirm external validity and determine accurate cutoff values for both children and adolescents. [14] (Sources: Guilleminault et al , 2011; Kane et al , 2025)

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: On physical examination, general appearance provides valuable diagnostic clues. Patients may appear fatigued or, conversely, exhibit hyperactivity. Findings may include allergic shiners, swollen nasal mucosa, micrognathia, macroglossia, high-arched palate, adenoidal facies, and tonsillar hypertrophy. Neurologic assessment should include evaluation of muscle tone, and cardiovascular examination should be performed to assess for pulmonary hypertension. [15]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- History and Physical
content: Hyponasal speech and nasal obstruction are frequently noted. Increasing rates of childhood obesity are a growing risk factor for pediatric OSA. Height, weight, and body mass index (BMI) should be measured at every clinical encounter, as each 1 kg/m² increase in BMI above the 50th percentile raises the risk for OSA by approximately 12%.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Nocturnal PSG is the diagnostic gold standard when the history and physical examination suggest pediatric OSA. However, PSG is resource-intensive, time-consuming, and costly, limiting its availability in many settings. Overnight home oximetry can provide supportive information but does not replace PSG for definitive diagnosis. When an underlying cardiopulmonary disorder is suspected, chest radiography and electrocardiography are recommended. A cardiac evaluation, including echocardiography, is particularly important before surgical intervention in children with severe OSA.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Emerging evidence indicates that specific inflammatory biomarkers, including kallikrein-1, uromodulin, urocortin-3, and orosomucoid-1, may be elevated in pediatric OSA and could enhance diagnostic precision. Routine laboratory evaluation may include a complete blood count, iron studies, and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels to identify alternative or contributing causes of sleep disturbance. Imaging studies can help delineate anatomic abnormalities predisposing to airway obstruction but should be interpreted in conjunction with PSG findings for diagnostic confirmation. [16]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Multiple physiologic parameters of sleep quality and quantity are recorded during PSG. Sensors measure electroencephalographic activity, heart rate, nasal and oral airflow, oxygen saturation, limb movements, ocular movements, and snoring intensity. These data are used to calculate sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, and time spent in each sleep stage.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: For the diagnosis of OSA, PSG quantifies the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI)—the average number of apneic and hypopneic episodes per hour of sleep. The interpretation of AHI differs between adults and children, with lower thresholds in pediatric populations representing more severe disease. AHI is the only standardized and scientifically accepted measure for grading OSA severity, providing an objective and reproducible metric. Table 2 presents the AHI grading criteria for assessing OSA severity in both pediatric and adult patients (see Table 2. Apnea-Hypopnea Index Criteria for Grading the Severity of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children and Adults). [17] An AHI of 1 or greater is considered abnormal in children aged 13 years and younger. However, the clinical significance of an AHI between 1 and 1.9 events per hour remains debated.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: For patients aged 13 to 17 years, either pediatric or adult criteria may be applied, depending on clinical context and developmental status. Since children generally have greater upper airway integrity and lower airway collapsibility than adults, PSG findings are often dominated by hypopneic events rather than complete apneas. Additionally, hypercarbia may occur in pediatric OSA due to prolonged hypoventilation, a feature less commonly seen in adult populations.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Pulse oximetry and home sleep apnea testing are alternative methods for monitoring SDB outside the laboratory setting. These approaches record fewer parameters than full PSG but may offer a more convenient and cost-effective option. Although home sleep apnea testing is an acceptable diagnostic tool for uncomplicated adult OSA, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) has found insufficient evidence to support its use in pediatric patients. [18] [19] [18]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Several radiologic modalities are available for the evaluation of the upper airway in suspected pediatric OSA, including lateral neck radiographs, cephalometric analysis, fluoroscopy, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These imaging techniques are primarily used in research, as well as in the clinical assessment of children with craniofacial abnormalities or neurological disorders, to identify the level of airway obstruction and guide management planning. However, radiation exposure associated with x-rays and CT scans, along with the limitations of airway evaluation in the awake state, restricts their use in routine pediatric assessment.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: Dynamic MRI and drug-induced sleep endoscopy have emerged as valuable alternatives for upper airway evaluation in children. Drug-induced sleep endoscopy involves the use of a flexible endoscope to visualize airway dynamics while the child is in a pharmacologically induced sleep-like state, providing direct visualization of obstruction sites (see Image . Evaluation of Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea). [20]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Evaluation
content: The AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events, Version 3 includes several key updates and new sections. Additions encompass the reporting of the highest and lowest heart rates during sleep, the central apnea index, and the duration below specified oxygen saturation thresholds. The updated version also recommends reporting the occurrence of snoring in children and introduces new sections addressing the multiple sleep latency test, maintenance of wakefulness test, and rules for scoring atrioventricular heart block, pacemaker rhythm, and arousals preceding transitions to wakefulness. (Source: AASM , 2023)

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment options for pediatric OSA vary according to disease severity and include both surgical and nonsurgical modalities. A therapeutic trial of leukotriene inhibitors, such as montelukast, may be considered in pediatric patients with mild-to-moderate OSA. [21]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Montelukast has demonstrated efficacy in reducing adenotonsillar size after approximately 3 months of therapy, resulting in a corresponding decrease in AHI in appropriately selected patients. [22] However, montelukast has been associated with serious neuropsychiatric adverse events, including suicidal ideation, depression, anxiety, agitation, and hallucinations. Since behavioral changes are also common in pediatric OSA, families and caregivers should be counseled to closely monitor for these symptoms and distinguish them from baseline behavioral manifestations. In March 2020, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration mandated a black box warning for montelukast due to its potential for serious mental health side effects. [23]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Systemic glucocorticoids have not shown benefit in the management of pediatric OSA. In contrast, intranasal corticosteroid therapy administered for 6 weeks has been shown to improve AHI and may be considered for patients with mild-to-moderate disease. When used in combination with leukotriene inhibitors, intranasal corticosteroids have been shown to produce a clinically significant reduction in AHI in most patients. [24]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: If adenotonsillar hypertrophy is present, the primary and most effective treatment is adenotonsillectomy. This procedure is recommended for most pediatric patients with an AHI greater than 9 events per hour, as well as those with mild-to-moderate disease accompanied by significant symptoms.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Partial tonsillectomy may be considered as an alternative approach, offering reduced postoperative complications and shorter recovery time. However, reported rates of tonsillar regrowth range from 7.2% to 16.6%. Other surgical procedures, including lingual tonsillectomy and uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, have limited evidence and have not demonstrated superiority over adenotonsillectomy. Although more conservative in scope, adenoidectomy alone has not shown superior outcomes compared with adenotonsillectomy in the management of pediatric OSA. The potential for recurrence of OSA and the need for repeat surgery following adenoidectomy should be carefully weighed in treatment planning. [25]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: A period of observation or “watchful waiting” for up to 6 months may be appropriate for patients with mild-to-moderate OSA. This approach allows for the management of underlying conditions such as obesity or allergic rhinitis, which may improve OSA and reduce AHI without surgical intervention. However, in pediatric patients without obesity or underlying syndromic conditions, adenotonsillectomy has been shown to produce superior improvement in AHI. [26]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is another potential treatment option. While CPAP is considered 1st-line therapy in adults, its use in children presents several limitations. CPAP should be considered during the perioperative period before adenotonsillectomy for severe OSA if the child is not a suitable surgical candidate, or moderate-to-severe OSA persists following surgery. Compliance can be challenging in pediatric patients, and prolonged use of the same mask may alter facial structure. CPAP is particularly indicated in children who have severe obesity, craniofacial abnormalities that preclude adenotonsillectomy, or residual OSA postoperatively.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: High-flow nasal cannula therapy represents an alternative for children who cannot tolerate CPAP. High-flow nasal cannula delivers heated, high-flow, humidified air through a nasal cannula, improving sleep quality and reducing respiratory events in children with OSA. [27]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: The AASM issued a position statement regarding CPAP in pediatric OSA, noting that CPAP may be safely and effectively used in the outpatient setting, particularly for children of young age or lower body weight. The statement emphasizes that clinicians with expertise in pediatric OSA should perform evaluation and management of CPAP therapy. [28]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Oral appliances have been shown to reduce AHI in adults. However, insufficient studies exist in pediatric populations to determine the efficacy of these tools or identify which patients might benefit. Adjusting oral appliances to accommodate a child’s growth would require frequent refittings. Rapid maxillary expansion may be considered in prepubescent patients and is particularly useful for children who have high-arched palates or do not have obesity but have residual OSA following adenotonsillectomy. [29]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Myofunctional therapy is an emerging approach in the management of both pediatric and adult OSA. This therapy involves retraining the muscles of the oral cavity and oropharyngeal structures, as well as optimizing tongue posture. Data on efficacy in children are limited, with only small pediatric studies reported. Nevertheless, myofunctional therapy is a potential adjunctive treatment and a focus for future research. [30]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with reversible risk factors for OSA, particularly obesity, should receive counseling on risk factor modification. Weight loss can improve OSA and serve as an adjunctive therapy in older children. Caregivers should also be advised to minimize exposure to secondhand smoke, as environmental tobacco exposure has been associated with an increased risk of pediatric OSA. [31]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Other upper airway surgeries beyond adenotonsillectomy are generally reserved for children with comorbidities causing multilevel airway obstruction. Persistent OSA following adenotonsillectomy may result from hypertrophy of the nasal turbinates, deviated nasal septum, adenoidal regrowth, lingual tonsil hypertrophy, or enlargement of the tongue base. Targeted surgical interventions addressing these specific anatomic abnormalities are required to relieve upper airway obstruction and resolve persistent OSA in affected children. [32]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: In pediatric patients with complex comorbidities, such as obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial abnormalities, or neuromuscular disorders, positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy may be implemented using CPAP, bilevel PAP, or invasive ventilation. Tracheotomy may be necessary in severe cases. [33]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Treatment / Management
content: Tracheotomy is the definitive surgical treatment for OSA. Most patients requiring tracheotomy have severe craniofacial anomalies or neuromuscular hypotonia. Although some children are tracheostomy-dependent, the procedure may also serve as a temporary intervention to manage severe OSA while awaiting additional surgical management. [34]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Pediatric OSA shares overlapping symptoms with multiple conditions. Accurate diagnosis and differentiation of OSA from these potential mimics require PSG.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis often contributes to snoring and should be managed accordingly. Behavioral manifestations such as hyperactivity or inattention can mimic attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, while learning difficulties may be mistaken for developmental delay. Nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux can produce brief breathing pauses and may exacerbate adenotonsillar hypertrophy, increasing OSA risk. Secondary nocturnal enuresis warrants evaluation for OSA. Morning headaches, often due to overnight carbon dioxide retention, require assessment for atypical features. Parasomnias may be increased but are not specific, and daytime sleepiness in older children should prompt consideration of narcolepsy.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Prognosis
content: Timely management of modifiable risk factors is essential to mitigate the long-term consequences of pediatric OSA. Interventions include weight management in children with overweight, optimal control of allergic rhinitis, and reduction of exposure to secondhand smoke. Adenotonsillectomy is the 1st-line treatment, while CPAP therapy may be appropriate for children who experience residual OSA or cannot undergo surgery. Untreated or persistent OSA can impair attention, learning, memory, quality of life, and emotional well-being. The condition also increases the risk of chronic conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes, and, in severe cases, may result in growth impairment and failure to thrive. [35]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Prognosis
content: Children at higher risk for OSA are also at increased risk of neurocognitive deficits later in life if the condition is unaddressed. Prompt identification and management can prevent long-term complications and preserve overall neurodevelopmental and physiological health.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Prognosis
content: After adenotonsillectomy, a period of up to 6 months is generally appropriate to allow inflammation to resolve and sleep patterns to normalize. Patients should be reassessed at that time for improvements in sleep quality and function. Routine postoperative PSG is usually unnecessary. Success may be evaluated based on improvements in initial behavioral or cognitive issues and reduced parental concern regarding observed sleep disturbances. If performed, postoperative PSG can provide objective data on AHI reductions. A comparative study of adenotonsillectomy versus watchful waiting demonstrated significant improvements in OSA symptoms, AHI, and behavior among surgical patients, although executive function and attention scores did not differ between groups.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Prognosis
content: The majority of children experience symptomatic improvement following adenotonsillectomy. Data indicate superior outcomes compared to watchful waiting, with normalization of PSG findings in 79% of surgical patients versus 46% with conservative management. In children with mild OSA (AHI >1), symptoms persist in 19% to 73% of cases. In severe OSA (AHI >5), persistent symptoms, including snoring and disrupted sleep, occur in only 13% to 29% of patients. Most children do not require long-term monitoring unless symptoms persist. Adenotonsillectomy is less effective in patients with Down syndrome, craniofacial abnormalities, or both. These children require postoperative surveillance and at least annual repeat PSG due to a high risk of persistent or recurrent OSA. Children with obesity also require weight management to optimize postoperative outcomes. [36]

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Complications
content: If left untreated, pediatric OSA may result in significant morbidity and long-term complications. Sustained hypoxia increases pulmonary vasoconstriction, which may lead to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure at an early age. Cognitive dysfunction, impaired learning, and poor school performance are frequently associated with undiagnosed or untreated pediatric OSA. Additionally, the increased work of breathing may contribute to failure to thrive, particularly in younger children.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Complications
content: Surgical intervention must be approached with caution, as adenotonsillectomy, while effective, is not without risk. Adverse events following tonsillectomy are uncommon but can occur. The most frequent postoperative complications include localized pain, reduced oral intake, and dehydration during the acute recovery period. More serious complications include bleeding, secondary infection, respiratory compromise, velopharyngeal insufficiency, and subglottic stenosis. As with any procedure involving airway management, patients may develop bronchospasm or laryngospasm. Furthermore, the severity of OSA is predictive of postoperative risk. Children with more severe disease may require prolonged observation in the postanesthesia care unit or inpatient monitoring following surgery.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Before diagnosis, parents should be educated during well-child visits to remain vigilant for signs and symptoms of pediatric OSA, including loud nightly snoring, frequent nighttime awakenings, secondary nocturnal enuresis, and behavioral changes. Additionally, caregivers of children with elevated body weight or a family history of obesity should receive guidance regarding the complications of adiposity, including the heightened risk of pediatric OSA.

content: Healthcare providers must emphasize the importance of recognizing sleep disturbances, as caregivers may not always perceive dysfunctional sleep patterns. An additional component of patient and caregiver education involves setting appropriate expectations regarding outcomes following adenotonsillectomy. Complete symptom resolution may not occur in children with obesity without concurrent weight reduction.

title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Children presenting with loud nightly snoring, fragmented sleep, and behavioral disturbances should be screened for OSA. A subset of patients may exhibit additional symptoms, including nocturnal enuresis, morning headaches, irritability, and declining academic performance. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and obtaining a detailed sleep history are essential to identify OSA in these cases.

content: Furthermore, all children being evaluated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder should be assessed for sleep quality and duration before the initiation of pharmacologic therapy. Given the rising prevalence of pediatric obesity, OSA, an important comorbidity of excessive adiposity, should be discussed routinely with caregivers during well-child visits.
